summary.title: Building a CHIP-8 Emulator [C++]
summary.one_liner: You learn how a CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions by building a working CHIP-8 emulator in C++ with SDL, step by step.
takeaways: A CPU reads encoded two-byte instructions from memory; an emulator decodes those and mimics the original machine's behavior on the host.
CHIP-8 components to emulate: 16 8-bit registers (V0-VF), 4K memory with ROM loaded at 0x200, 16-level stack, delay and sound timers, 16 keys, and a 64x32 monochrome display.
Drawing works by XORing sprite pixels onto the display, which sets VF on collision and explains why moving sprites flicker.
Opcodes can be decoded with a function pointer table indexed by the first nibble, with secondary tables for opcodes sharing a first digit.
The project uses SDL for rendering and input, with command-line options for scale, cycle delay and ROM file.
summary.summary: The author walks through building a CHIP-8 emulator in C++, starting with a primer on how CPUs and assembly work and then describing the CHIP-8's registers, memory map, stack, timers, keypad and display. The code is developed in sections covering ROM loading, font loading, random numbers, each of the 34 instructions, and a function-pointer table for opcode decoding. A platform layer uses SDL for rendering and input, and a main loop takes scale, delay and ROM arguments. The article ends by testing with a test ROM and Tetris, and it includes an appendix on bits and bytes. It is aimed at inexperienced programmers who know basic C++.
